newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Report cites 35,000 west African religious slaves.
newsitem.headline: Report cites 35,000 west African religious slaves.

text.p: Australia's Anti-Slavery Society said on Monday that there were up to 35,000 religious slaves in west Africa, with some girls as young as eight forced to perform sexual acts for holy men to appease traditional gods.
The report called "The Forgotten Girl-Slaves of West Africa" said the girls were the modern version of religious slaves formerly offered as human sacrifices.

"Originally offered as human sacrifice to ensure success in war, these girls are the helpless victims of a traditional form of slavery in which they are known locally as 'fetish slaves'," the report said.
"The girls are offered as slaves in order to appease the gods and to atone for wrongs committed by their relatives, usually male relations," said the report released on Monday.

The report, compiled by an Australian lawyer during a visit to west Africa in November 1995, estimated there were 29,000 to 35,000 fetish slaves in the region, principally in Ghana and to a lesser extent Togo, Benin and Nigeria.
It said the girls were given voluntarily by their parents to holy men to perform domestic chores at shrines and sexual acts.

The report published testimonies and photographs of girls as young as seven and of an 86-year-old woman who said she had been a slave all her life. Many of the girls said they had two or three children by their "fetish priest."
Elizabeth Evatt, Australia's member on the U.N. Human Rights Committee, said the report was the first to examine religious slavery.

"It is a tragedy that there are still so many girl-slaves in west Africa, over 150 years after slavery was abolished," Evatt said during the launch of the report. "These girl-children...are slaves in the fullest sense of the term," Evatt said.
The anti-slavery society, which watches Africa and Asia, had been invited to west Africa by African community leaders and non-governmental organisations.

Paul Bravender-Coyle, the author of the report, said the definition of slavery used in the report was not the classic form where a person is bought and sold, but where a person's liberty is controlled by another.
Bravender-Coyle said Australia's Anti-Slavery Society was raising funds and negotiating with fetish priests to buy some of the girls out of slavery.
"We do not know how much it will cost because it has never been done before, but it is cheaper to buy in bulk, 12 to 15 at a time," Bravender-Coyle told Reuters.
Bravender-Coyle called on the former west African colonial powers Britain, Germany and France to provide assistance to eradicate religious slavery.
"The local priests wield enormous power. The long-term solution is to educate the people and the priests," he said.
